1: 50 Hz: the whole cable has the same voltage at any moment, it is just a wire
2: 100 MHz: the voltage already differs along the cable
3: 1 GHz: five waves fit on 1 m, the signal travels along the cable as a wave
4: Rule of thumb: longer than 1/10 of the wavelength → treat it as a transmission line
5: What does the wave see? Every centimetre of cable is a small L and a small C
6: You know: L and C change their impedance with frequency
7: Along the ladder only their ratio counts: ω cancels out
8: Typical coax: L′ ≈ 250 nH/m, C′ ≈ 100 pF/m → Z₀ = √2500 = 50 Ω
9: Z₀ is the characteristic impedance: no loss, the same for any length and frequency
10: At the end of the line the wave meets the load. If the load is not Z₀, part of it comes back.
